claims.sentence: The NHS says a colonoscopy is often done to find the cause of bowel symptoms.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus (US source) says doctors order colonoscopy for symptoms such as abdominal pain, changes in bowel movements or weight loss. The NHS wording was not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A colonoscopy is often done to look for the cause of bowel symptoms, such as abdominal pain or a change in bowel habit.

claims.sentence: Other reasons include looking for early signs of bowel cancer in people at high risk, and checking after earlier treatment for bowel cancer.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus (US) lists follow-up of earlier polyps or colon cancer. 'Early signs in people at high risk' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Colonoscopy is also used to follow up after earlier polyps or bowel cancer, according to MedlinePlus, a US source.

claims.sentence: People who have had polyps removed before, or who have a family history of bowel cancer, may also be referred.
claims.evidence: Retrieved PMC text: repeat colonoscopy is routinely recommended after polyp removal; family history at least doubles risk. No text on referral for family history.
claims.newSentence: People who have had polyps removed before are routinely advised to have repeat colonoscopies.

claims.sentence: For a clear view, the bowel needs to be empty.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus: the colon must be emptied first because problems may be missed if the intestines are not cleaned out (US source).

claims.sentence: Trusts generally prescribe a laxative solution, often a powder mixed with water, to empty the bowel.
claims.evidence: Laxatives are mentioned (MedlinePlus, US) but 'trusts generally' and 'powder mixed with water' were not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Preparation can include laxatives to empty the bowel.

claims.sentence: One trust describes the preparation as taking laxatives, cutting down on fibre, and stopping all food in the last few hours beforehand.
claims.evidence: Not retrieved for a specific trust. MedlinePlus (US) says prep can include enemas, clear liquids the day before and laxatives.
claims.newSentence: Preparation can include clear liquids the day before and laxatives, according to MedlinePlus, a US source.

claims.sentence: Leaflets warn of frequent diarrhoea, cramping and nausea, and advise staying near a toilet.
claims.evidence: A review (PMC) lists vomiting, colicky stomach ache and dizziness among the most common prep problems; diarrhoea and 'stay near a toilet' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A review of bowel preparation lists vomiting, colicky stomach ache and dizziness among the most common problems.

claims.sentence: One trust notes that the laxative can cause dehydration, light-headedness, low blood pressure or kidney problems.
claims.evidence: Review did not give kidney problems or low blood pressure from prep; not confirmed.

claims.sentence: Preparation details differ between trusts, and the hospital sends its own instructions.
claims.evidence: Only partly: MedlinePlus says the type of prep depends on what the doctor recommends. 'Hospital sends own instructions' not retrieved verbatim.
claims.newSentence: Preparation depends on which type the doctor recommends, and it can differ between hospitals.

claims.sentence: A nurse sees the person first to discuss their medical history, carry out simple checks and explain what will happen.
claims.evidence: NHS pages: a nurse checks details, explains the procedure and risks, and checks pulse, blood pressure and oxygen levels.

claims.sentence: A thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed through the anus and around the large bowel.
claims.evidence: NHS pages: a thin, flexible tube with a camera goes in through the anus.

claims.sentence: Air is pumped in to open the bowel, which can cause bloating or cramps.
claims.evidence: NHS pages: air or gas is passed through the tube to open the bowel; can cause bloating and cramping.

claims.sentence: The NHS says a colonoscopy can be uncomfortable but should not be painful.
claims.evidence: NHS says the camera may be felt going in but it should not hurt; cramping is common. One trust leaflet warns it can sometimes be quite painful.

claims.sentence: The procedure itself takes about 30 to 45 minutes, and a person may be at the hospital for about two hours in total.
claims.evidence: NHS England says it should take 30 to 45 minutes and you might be at the hospital for around 2 hours. Other trusts quote different times; unattributed sentence should name the source.
claims.newSentence: NHS England says a colonoscopy should take 30 to 45 minutes, and a person may be at the hospital for around two hours in total.

claims.sentence: A leaflet says some people have sedation, some breathe a pain-relieving gas called Entonox, and some have no pain relief.
claims.evidence: Trust pages: choice of sedation, Entonox (gas and air) or neither.

claims.sentence: Sedation is given through a small needle in the back of the hand.
claims.evidence: Sources say sedation goes through a cannula in the hand or arm; 'needle in back of hand' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Sedation is given through a thin tube called a cannula in the hand or arm.

claims.sentence: Polyps are growths on the bowel lining, and they are usually not cancer.
claims.evidence: PMC text: most polyps are benign; hyperplastic polyps carry no cancer risk, adenomas can progress.

claims.sentence: It is not possible to tell by looking whether a polyp contains cancer cells, so polyps are removed and examined under a microscope.
claims.evidence: PMC text: the physician usually cannot tell polyp type by eye, so suspicious polyps are usually removed and sent for microscope examination. 'Not possible' is stronger than retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Doctors usually cannot tell the type of polyp just by looking, so suspicious polyps are usually removed and examined under a microscope.

claims.sentence: Staff can also take small tissue samples, called biopsies, which is painless.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus (US) and trusts: tissue samples are taken with forceps or snare and patients typically do not feel it.
claims.newSentence: Staff can also take small tissue samples, called biopsies, which people typically do not feel.

claims.sentence: Afterwards the person is usually told whether any polyps were removed or samples taken.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus (US): some findings are shared after sedation wears off; 'usually told whether polyps removed' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Some findings may be shared once the sedation has worn off, according to MedlinePlus, a US source.

claims.sentence: The NHS describes colonoscopy as a common and straightforward procedure.
claims.evidence: Not retrieved as an NHS statement. Trust leaflets describe colonoscopy as very safe with serious complications rare.
claims.newSentence: NHS trust leaflets describe colonoscopy as very safe, with serious complications rare.

claims.sentence: The main risks are a tear in the bowel wall, called perforation, and bleeding.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus (US) and trust leaflets: bleeding and perforation are the main complications.

claims.sentence: Trust leaflets give perforation figures that differ, and one says it happens to about one person in 1,000 nationally.
claims.evidence: Trust leaflets give about 1 in 1,500, less than 1 in 1,700 and about 1 in 1,000 procedures. 'Nationally' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Trust leaflets give perforation figures that differ, and one says about 1 in 1,000 procedures.

claims.sentence: The risk rises when polyps are removed, especially large or complex ones.
claims.evidence: Trust leaflets: polyp removal raises bleeding and perforation risk; one gives 1 in 500 to 1 in 20 depending on polyp size, location and difficulty.

claims.sentence: Sometimes a hole can be closed with clips during the procedure.
claims.evidence: Clip closure not retrieved. Leaflets say repair often needs surgery; one says antibiotics and rest can sometimes settle it.
claims.newSentence: A perforation is treated in hospital, and surgery is sometimes needed, according to NHS trust leaflets.

claims.sentence: It is common to pass a small amount of blood from the anus after a biopsy or polyp removal.
claims.evidence: Trust leaflets: small amounts of blood are expected after biopsy or polyp removal; North Tees says it can occur up to 2 weeks later.

claims.sentence: Colonoscopy is very accurate, but occasionally a problem, including rarely a cancer, can be missed.
claims.evidence: Frimley leaflet: chance of missing cancer or a polyp approx 3 in 100; other trusts say occasional, rarely cancer. 'Very accurate' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Trust leaflets say a colonoscopy can occasionally miss a problem, including, rarely, a cancer.

claims.sentence: Severe belly pain, heavy bleeding or a fever after the test needs urgent help: NHS 111 or the hospital unit, and 999 if it is severe.
claims.evidence: NHS colonoscopy page: call 111 or the hospital for some symptoms, 999 or A&E for more serious ones; full symptom list not retrieved, so specific symptoms (fever, heavy bleeding) not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to call NHS 111 or the hospital where the test was done for some symptoms after a colonoscopy, and to call 999 or go to A&E for more serious ones; its page lists which symptoms apply.

claims.sentence: A letter or call with the results usually comes two to three weeks after a colonoscopy.
claims.evidence: NHS trust pages: letter or call about 2 to 3 weeks after; other trusts quote longer waits for biopsy results.
claims.newSentence: Some NHS trusts say a letter or call with the results comes about two to three weeks after a colonoscopy, though waits can differ.

claims.sentence: A normal result means no polyps or cancer were found in the bowel.
claims.evidence: Not retrieved. Sources say the results say whether things are normal or need treatment; a normal result does not exclude a missed finding (leaflets note missed problems).
claims.newSentence: The result will say whether anything abnormal was found and whether further treatment is needed, according to NHS trust pages.

claims.sentence: If a biopsy was taken, the biopsy results can take up to two weeks.
claims.evidence: Retrieved waits for biopsy/polyp results: several days, usually within 2-3 weeks, 4-6 weeks, 8-10 weeks. 'Up to two weeks' not supported.
claims.newSentence: If a biopsy was taken, trust leaflets give differing waits for the biopsy results, from several days to several weeks.

claims.sentence: A colonoscopy passes a thin, flexible tube with a camera through the bowel to look for the cause of symptoms, to screen for bowel cancer, or to follow up earlier problems.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus (US): symptoms and follow-up of polyps/cancer; screening shown by NHS England bowel screening guide and Frimley 'Bowel Cancer Screening' colonoscopy leaflet (titles/snippets).

claims.sentence: The bowel must be empty for a clear view, so a laxative preparation is taken beforehand and often causes frequent diarrhoea.
claims.evidence: Empty bowel supported (MedlinePlus, US); 'often causes frequent diarrhoea' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The bowel must be empty for a clear view, so a bowel preparation, which can include laxatives, is taken beforehand.

claims.sentence: Polyps, which are growths on the bowel lining, can be removed during the test and examined under a microscope.
claims.evidence: Polyps are removed (snare/forceps) and suspicious ones examined under a microscope (PMC; MedlinePlus).

claims.sentence: Perforation, a tear in the bowel wall, is the main serious risk and is uncommon, with higher risk when polyps are removed.
claims.evidence: Trust leaflets: bleeding and perforation are the main risks, serious complications rare; polyp removal raises risk.

claims.sentence: A colonoscopy uses a thin camera to look inside the large bowel. This guide covers bowel preparation, sedation, risks and when results arrive.
claims.evidence: Descriptive summary; thin camera looking inside the large bowel is basic fact, listed topics match the body.

notes: Search summaries were lossy; MedlinePlus and PMC are US/academic. Extra facts: NHS England says test takes 30 to 45 min, ~2 hours at hospital (https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/your-guide-to-nhs-bowel-cancer-screening/); trust leaflets say bleeding can occur up to 2 weeks after (https://www.nth.nhs.uk/resources/colonoscopy/); Frimley leaflet puts missed cancer/polyp chance at about 3 in 100 (https://www.fhft.nhs.uk/patients-and-visitors/patient-information-library/colonoscopy-bowel-cancer-screening); Entonox can be breathed in and controlled by the patient, wearing off in about 30 minutes (https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/colonoscopy/what-happens-on-the-day/). Triage wording and sedation-after-care were not fully retrieved.
